chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Traditional Portfolio Construction Fails

lessons.title: From Naive Diversification to Risk-Based Diversification

children.text: Two lessons in, you have two reasons to distrust the standard mean-variance workflow: it amplifies small errors in return forecasts into wildly different portfolios, and even if you dodge the forecasting problem entirely, capital weights and risk weights are not the same thing. This lesson asks the obvious next question. What if you just stop forecasting and stop optimizing altogether? Split your money equally and walk away. How far does that get you, and what is still missing.
Naive Diversification: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of 1/N

markDefs.definition: Splitting capital equally across N assets, with no return forecasts, no covariance estimates, and no optimization at all.

children.text: could not be simpler: with N assets, put 1/N of your capital in each. No expected returns, no covariance matrix, nothing to estimate at all. On paper this looks primitive next to a Markowitz optimizer. In practice, it has held up embarrassingly well.

body.text: In a widely cited 2009 study, 'Optimal Versus Naive Diversification,' Victor DeMiguel, Lorenzo Garlappi, and Raman Uppal tested mean-variance optimization and several of its refinements against the plain 1/N portfolio across 14 empirical datasets. The naive 1/N portfolio frequently matched or beat the optimized portfolios out of sample. The reason connects directly to the last lesson: 1/N has zero estimation error, because it estimates nothing. An optimizer that amplifies small input mistakes can lose to a strategy that simply refuses to make any estimates worth getting wrong.

children.text: Sidestepping estimation error does not sidestep the capital weight versus risk contribution gap from the last lesson. 1/N splits money equally. It says nothing about volatility. Extend the earlier two-asset example to three: Nifty 50 equity, 10-year G-Sec debt, and gold, using the same illustrative long-run assumptions as before plus a gold volatility of 12% and modest, realistic correlations.

body.caption: 1/N portfolio: equal capital weight vs actual risk contribution (illustrative)

body.text: An equal-money, three-way split across equity, debt, and gold is not an equal-risk portfolio. Under these illustrative assumptions, equity alone still drives more than half of total portfolio volatility, and debt, despite holding a full third of the capital, barely moves the needle. 1/N fixes the estimation-error problem from lesson 1. It does nothing about the risk concentration problem from lesson 2.

children.text: The most direct fix that still avoids return forecasting is to weight each asset in inverse proportion to its own volatility. A more volatile asset gets less capital, a calmer asset gets more, so that each asset's own risk, on a standalone basis, is roughly offset by its weight.

body.caption: Inverse-volatility weighting. Each asset's weight is proportional to the reciprocal of its own volatility, so a doubling of volatility roughly halves the weight.

children.text: Apply this to the same three assets. Nifty 50's volatility of 14% is the highest of the three, so it gets the smallest weight. The 10-year G-Sec's volatility of 5% is the lowest, so it gets the largest weight, even larger than its 1/N share. Gold sits in between.

body.caption: 1/N vs inverse-volatility weighting: capital weights and resulting risk contribution (illustrative)

body.title: Risk contribution share by weighting scheme (illustrative)

children.text: That is a real improvement. Moving from 1/N to inverse-volatility weighting took the risk contribution spread from roughly 54/5/41 to roughly 33/31/36, much closer to an even three-way split, using nothing more than each asset's own volatility. No covariance estimates, no return forecasts, just one number per asset.
Why Inverse-Vol Isn't the Finish Line

Look closely at the inverse-vol risk contribution column: 33%, 31%, 36%. Close to an even split, but not exactly equal. The gap exists because inverse-volatility weighting only looks at each asset's own volatility. It ignores how the assets move together entirely. Gold's mild positive correlation with equity nudges its effective risk contribution up. Debt's negative correlation with equity nudges its effective risk contribution down, even after inverse-vol weighting already gave it the largest capital share.

Getting risk contributions to come out exactly equal, not approximately equal, requires solving a system of equations that accounts for the full covariance matrix, correlations included, simultaneously for every asset. That exact solution is what the finance literature calls Equal Risk Contribution, or risk parity in its purest form, and it is the subject of the next chapter.

body.title: From Mean-Variance to Risk Parity: A Short History

events.title: Markowitz Publishes 'Portfolio Selection'
events.description: The mean-variance framework from lesson 1 becomes the foundation of modern portfolio theory, and its estimation sensitivity becomes an open problem almost immediately.

events.title: Bridgewater Associates Launches All Weather
events.description: One of the earliest large-scale institutional implementations of risk-balanced, rather than capital-balanced, portfolio construction.

events.title: 'Risk Parity' Enters the Mainstream Vocabulary
events.description: Edward Qian's research popularizes equal risk contribution as a formal, named portfolio construction approach distinct from mean-variance optimization.

events.title: The Global Financial Crisis
events.description: Capital-weighted 'balanced' portfolios that behaved like concentrated equity bets in the crash push institutional investors toward risk-based diversification.

events.title: DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal Formalize Naive Diversification's Strength
events.description: Their study gives an empirical, estimation-error explanation for why simple 1/N so often held its own against optimized portfolios.

body.code:
import numpy as np

def risk_contributions(weights, cov):
    weights = np.array(weights)
    port_vol = np.sqrt(weights @ cov @ weights)
    mctr = (cov @ weights) / port_vol
    rc = weights * mctr
    return port_vol, rc / port_vol

# Nifty 50, 10-year G-Sec, Gold - illustrative annualized inputs
vol = np.array([0.14, 0.05, 0.12])
corr = np.array([
    [1.00, -0.10, 0.05],
    [-0.10, 1.00, 0.00],
    [0.05, 0.00, 1.00],
])
cov = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr

n = len(vol)
equal_weights = np.full(n, 1 / n)
inv_vol_weights = (1 / vol) / np.sum(1 / vol)

for name, w in [('1/N', equal_weights), ('Inverse-vol', inv_vol_weights)]:
    port_vol, rc_share = risk_contributions(w, cov)
    print(f"{name}: weights={np.round(w, 3)}  vol={port_vol:.2%}  risk contribution={np.round(rc_share * 100, 1)}%")
body.caption: Run this with your own volatility and correlation estimates from real NSE, G-Sec, and gold ETF (such as an MCX or NSE-listed gold ETF) return series. You will see the same pattern: inverse-vol weighting gets you much closer to equal risk contribution than 1/N, but rarely exactly there, because it never looks at correlation.

body.title: Where Inverse-Vol Still Falls Short
body.scenario: In the three-asset example, gold's risk contribution under inverse-volatility weighting came out at roughly 36%, higher than equity's roughly 33% and debt's roughly 31%, even though inverse-vol weighting gave gold less capital than debt.
body.prompt: Using only the correlation assumptions given (equity-debt -0.10, equity-gold 0.05, debt-gold 0.00), explain why gold's risk contribution ends up the highest of the three despite its middling volatility and middling capital weight.
body.modelAnswer: Correlation is the missing ingredient inverse-vol weighting never looks at. Debt has a negative correlation with equity, so debt's presence actually reduces total portfolio variance, which lowers debt's effective risk contribution below what its capital weight alone would suggest. Gold has a positive, not negative, correlation with equity, so instead of offsetting equity's risk the way debt does, gold's moves reinforce it slightly, pushing gold's effective risk contribution up. Inverse-vol weighting only sees each asset's own volatility, not this reinforcing or offsetting relationship with the rest of the portfolio, which is exactly why it cannot land on exactly equal risk contribution.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why did the 2009 DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal study find that the naive 1/N portfolio often matched or beat mean-variance optimized portfolios out of sample?
options: Because 1/N portfolios have lower transaction costs than optimized portfolios
Because 1/N requires no estimation of expected returns or covariances, so it carries none of the estimation error that the last lesson showed optimizers amplify
Because SEBI regulations favor equal-weighted portfolios for retail investors
Because mean-variance optimization always produces negative expected returns
body.explanation: 1/N's advantage is not that it is a smarter allocation rule, it is that it has zero estimation error because it estimates nothing. When an optimizer's edge from using better inputs is smaller than the damage caused by those inputs being wrong, as lesson 1 showed it often is, a rule that avoids estimation entirely can win by default.

cards.definition: Michaud's term for mean-variance optimizers, which treat every input as certain and therefore amplify small errors in expected return and covariance estimates into large, unstable weight changes.
An optimizer output that sits at the edge of the allowed range, such as a large concentrated long or short position, rather than a moderate interior weight.
The share of a portfolio's rupee value invested in a given asset.
The share of a portfolio's total volatility attributable to a given asset, accounting for its own volatility and its correlation with the rest of the portfolio.
Splitting capital equally across all assets with no forecasting or optimization, which sidesteps estimation error entirely but still ignores volatility and correlation differences.
Weighting each asset in inverse proportion to its own standalone volatility, an improvement over 1/N that still ignores correlations between assets.

body.text: Naive diversification fixes estimation error by estimating nothing, and inverse-volatility weighting improves on it by using each asset's own volatility. Neither one accounts for how assets move together, which is why neither lands on exactly equal risk contribution. Closing that last gap, correlation and all, is precisely what risk parity does, starting in the next chapter.

points: 1/N diversification avoids the estimation-error problem from lesson 1 entirely, since it forecasts nothing, and empirical research (DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal, 2009) shows it often matches optimized portfolios out of sample as a result.

1/N still inherits the capital-versus-risk gap from lesson 2: equal money does not mean equal risk, as the three-asset Nifty 50, G-Sec, and gold example showed (roughly 54/5/41 risk split from an equal 33/33/33 capital split).
Inverse-volatility weighting, sizing each asset inversely to its own volatility, meaningfully closes that gap using only one number per asset, no covariance matrix required.

Inverse-vol weighting still falls short of exactly equal risk contribution because it ignores correlation. Assets that offset the rest of the portfolio (negative correlation) end up with lower effective risk contribution than their weight suggests, and assets that reinforce it (positive correlation) end up higher.
Solving for weights that make every asset's risk contribution come out exactly equal, using the full covariance matrix, is the formal definition of risk parity, and it is where the course goes next.
